claims.claim: Ruby threads release the GVL during network I/O, so a Sidekiq thread blocked on a slow customer isn't burning CPU
claims.about: Ruby (Sidekiq threads; closest measured stack is ruby-rails)
claims.measured: ruby-rails I/O wait test (10 ms upstream wait, 256 connections): 17% CPU at 279 req/s, p50 903 ms
claims.why: The only measured Ruby stack used just 17% CPU while its requests waited on I/O, so blocked Ruby threads were not burning CPU; Sidekiq itself was not measured, and the very low throughput shows its limit is how many requests it can hold at once, not CPU.

claims.claim: Go's real advantage is cheap concurrency: thousands of in-flight connections in one small process, with no per-thread memory cost
claims.measured: I/O wait test, 256 connections: go-gin 20,235 req/s at 16 MB peak, go-nethttp 18,905 req/s at 15 MB, against ruby-rails 279 req/s at 185 MB
claims.why: At 256 connections the Go servers kept about 200 requests in flight in about 16 MB and handled about 70 times Rails' throughput, which supports cheap concurrency in a small process; 'thousands' of connections goes beyond the 256 that were measured.
